title: How wise is it to make complex mechanics without coding? Just eventing, etc.

posts.author: WingedHares
posts.body:
Hey, y'all! An idea popped into my head recently about making mechanics just out of eventing, existing plugins, etc. This is because I'm anxious about commissioning new coders due to my last one disappearing on me, costing me a couple hundred dollars and leaving me with a buggy plugin I can't safely use.
I'd comm others, but seeing as mechanics are a core part of games, I just don't feel great leaving it to people who might disappear again. This way I can also tweak them exactly the way I want.
So, I tried learning to code myself and sadly, it got nowhere since I already have too much tasks on my plate to learn a whole other subject. But I know my way around eventing and I'm confident I can use existing plugins to make new mechanics as I've done something similar in the past, but it makes me wonder if it's even wise to pursue as it potentially can get quite complex. Like, would it be taxing on the game, making for slow fps, etc? My game is quite art-centric as well.
For reference, the most potentially complex mechanic I'd like to make is a turn-based battle system with light rhythm gameplay. Without coding, that would mean not using/overhauling the default battle system and starting over from scratch with just eventing, script calls, and existing plugins. My game is a visual novel hybrid, so I'd likely make it simpler than your usual turn-based mechanics, but I feel implementing it would still be fairly complex.
I don't know. Maybe it's a silly question with an obvious answer for the veterans here, haha, but yeah, do you think it's wiser to just commission coders or should I give this method a try? Especially would like to hear from those who've tried it themselves!
If the latter, do you have any tips and tricks? Things to watch out for, etc.
Thanks in advance! Hope the thread will be useful for those wondering and new to this as well ^^
~ Nameless L.W. of WingedHares

posts.author: gstv87
posts.body:
coding is meant for the highest level of control... things that happen globally, at irregular intervals or without the player's influence.
eventing is for things that run at map level, mainly scene flow and one-off events.
you can't efficiently control the higher level of the whole game from the inferior level of a game scene.
it's not impossible, but it's a stretch, especially if the same thing can be done (or HAS been done) by coding.

posts.author: FleshToDust
posts.body: I have heard of very impressive things being made in RPG Maker 2003, long before the introduction of scripts or plugins. If you can code, do it but if not, try your hand at eventing if that is your only path to making the thing you require.

posts.author: lianderson
posts.body:
Normally I'd say, go for it, because there's a lot that can be made with eventing, more so than most devs realize.
However, it's a rhythm game, so there may be some input lag if done with events. If that occurs, be extra generous on the timings.

posts.author: AquaEcho
posts.body:
I have a ton of custom mechanics I  coded myself. Some of the scripts are in the engine, some in plugin files. I only have a few standalone plugins, most of what I do is tweaks to existing plugins.
Eventing has a lot of limitations. Some things you can technically event but it's more annoying, e.g. having to nest conditionals instead of compound them in one statement. The more dynamic or variable something is the more code I need. I have a lot of event AI. If I want an event to move somewhere, but where that is depends on a lot of factors, e.g. distance to the player or other events, checking for obstacles in the way, whether the target is still there or dead, etc, I need to do that in code, not eventing.

posts.author: Andar
posts.body:
It completely depends on what the mechanic is doing.
There are things that are better done as events, and other that are better done as plugin or scripts.
and some that are best done as a mix of both
Most battle-systems are usually done as plugins/scripts, but there are several completely evented battlesystems as well - it depends partially on complexity and partially on how many features (especially skills) of the database are to be used.

It will be a lot cheaper to use existing plugins. Even if you want edits, those edits will be far cheaper than commissioning a new plugin from scratch.
Whether something is taxing on the game or not- that's generally not an issue unless there's a memory leak somewhere, or you have a bunch of events running parallel every frame without waits. The things I've seen that can be taxing is pathfinding and lighting, maybe parallax maps could do it too.

posts.body: I think you are on the right track if your game is full of unique ideas. Go for it.

posts.author: Noxyy
posts.body:
You can't event a rythm game, the beat will go off-sync as soon as anything weird happens such as framerate dropping, code stopping, or whatever. You will need a plugin for that.
I wrote one for the
last game I made
, it's quite simlpe but not 'user friendly' like normal plugins 'cause I just wrote it for my own project. You can use it if you want, here's the
download link
.
First time you call the plugin, call these parameters moment the song starts playing:
AudioManager.setBPM(116)  //Replace 116 with your song's BPM
AudioManager.noxyStartCountingBPM();
AudioManager.noxyLoopBPM();
It will look like this in an event:
Afterwards, any time you want to change the song, just call these parameters:
AudioManager.noxyStopLoop();
AudioManager.setBPM(79); //Change BPM to the BPM of the new song
AudioManager.noxyStartCountingBPM();
It would look like this in an event:
To check if a player succesfully clicked or interacting with something to the rhytm of the song, just add a conditional branch like this:
(can be called in a parallell or normal 'action button' event, does not matter)
'noxyIsClickOnBeat' returns true it has been called within the 'grace period', otherwise it returns false.
The 'grace period' is how many tenths of a second you have after the beat has gone-by. We need a grace period because otherwise it becomes almost impossible to click 'on beat'.
If you want to change the grace period just edit this line in the plugin file:
The grace period is basically 'how big of a window' you have to click 'on beat'. 0.2 is a decent value, higher than that becomes too easy and lower than that starts to become quite hard real fast.
If you want a demo of the plugin working, here's a little video making use of the rhytm feature in my game:
(The cookies around the screen change to the rhytm. You can trigger anything to happen to the rhytm)
You can pretty much use any song you want, as long as you know it's tempo, if you add the wrong tempo to a song, it will be off-sync but that's about it.
